api.route.settings.openCode.description: Valid for 10 minutes, usable once; the answer includes a link that opens the local web page (the passcode comes after the #, so it stays out of server logs).
api.route.settings.openCode.exempt: Called by the local command daisy open (local-api.md section 1); not a separate subcommand
api.route.settings.openCode.notLetIn: Issues a one-time passcode for the local face: the local face listens only on the loopback address, so only someone on this machine can get it
api.route.settings.openCode.summary: Issue a one-time passcode for the local face (used by daisy open)
api.route.settings.openCodeExternal.desc: Whoever gets it can open the web page as the owner over the network, so it counts as "letting someone in" and needs the PIN. Answers 409 when the outside face is neither listening nor has a relay. When listening is on, the link is direct and the relay link is given separately (`relayUrl`; the relay operator could forge certificates, and `relayWarning` says so plainly); with only a relay, the relay link is given and the warning stated plainly; when the relay has only a self-signed certificate, no link is given (`url: null`) and the passcode is typed in by hand on the other machine.
api.route.settings.openCodeExternal.exem: Called by the local command daisy open --external (local-api.md section 1); not a separate subcommand
api.route.settings.openCodeExternal.summ: Issue a one-time passcode for the outside face (open the web page from another machine)
api.route.settings.pair.description: A kind of "letting someone in" (kind device): needs the PIN; the AI cannot do it. A pairing code is valid for {devicePairCodeMinutes} minutes, works once, and only on the outside face (first turn on the outside face's listener or choose a relay, both with the PIN). The answer holds the code itself and a link (the code is after #, so it never reaches the request line or the logs; the web page draws it as a QR code). With the outside face's listener on, the link is direct (a relay operator could get a certificate for the relay's address), and the relay's link is given separately (`relayUrl`, `relayWarning`); with only a relay, the relay's link is given and `warning` says plainly that the relay operator can obtain the pairing code and the device credential; when the relay has only a self-signed certificate no link is given (`url: null`), just the code to type in on the device, with a warning not to click through certificate warnings. At most {devicePendingCodesMax} unused codes at once; making another pushes out the oldest. {deviceRedeemFailuresMax} wrong codes from one source (the direct listener's address; through a relay, the address the relay reports) pause that source for {deviceRedeemLockMinutes} minutes (other sources go on); {deviceCodeWrongMax} wrong codes from all sources together void the codes of that period. `wasLocked` and `recentFailures` in the answer say someone typed a wrong code. Resetting or changing the PIN voids the unused codes and lifts the pauses too.
api.route.settings.pair.summary: Make a pairing code ({command} pair): another device that enters it connects as the owner
api.route.settings.pairRedeem.descriptio: Only on the outside face (the same for calls passed in through a connected relay). A right, unexpired, unused pairing code → the new device's record, a device credential (`ddev_…`, only ever in this one answer, kept on the device) and a device session (`dweb_…`, {deviceSessionHours} hours). A wrong, expired or used code is always 401 code_invalid, without saying which; {deviceRedeemFailuresMax} wrong codes from one source pause that source (423 pair_locked); a code typed wrong {deviceCodeWrongMax} times in all while valid is voided. At most {deviceRedeemPerMinute} calls per address per minute.
api.route.settings.pairRedeem.exempt: Used by the web page on another device (a phone browser) to exchange a pairing code for a credential (entered on the outside face's web page); the command line uses the local credential and needs no pairing
api.route.settings.pairRedeem.notLetIn: A device exchanges a pairing code for its own credential: the pairing code itself is issued by an endpoint that needs the PIN (daisy pair) and can be used only once
api.route.settings.pairRedeem.summary: Another device exchanges a pairing code for a device credential and its first device session
api.route.settings.passcode.description: auto: on when this machine has other people's accounts or the outside face is on. Changing this setting may widen who can open the web page, so it needs the PIN.
api.route.settings.passcode.summary: Set the local web page's passcode: auto (default), on, off
api.route.settings.pinGrant.description: A grant is valid for {pinGrantMinutes} minutes, and only for the credential that traded for it; a request that needs the PIN carries it in the `daisy-pin-grant` request header. {pinAttemptsPerRound} wrong PINs in a row lock entry (15 minutes; another wrong round 1 hour; then doubling each round, at most 24 hours); one right PIN clears it. The command line never caches a grant: every command that needs the PIN asks for it there and then, and the grant lives only in that command process's memory. The AI cannot call it.
api.route.settings.pinGrant.exempt: The command line does not get grants separately: each command that needs the PIN prompts for it on the spot, gets a grant, and discards it after use (local-api.md §6), so the grant never lands in terminal output, shell history or files
api.route.settings.pinGrant.notLetIn: Exchanging the PIN for a grant itself: it is the PIN that is required, so it cannot also require a PIN grant
api.route.settings.pinGrant.summary: Enter the PIN to get a short-lived PIN grant
api.route.settings.pinReset.description: Only done on the local command line (local credential); the web page, paired devices and the AI cannot call it. A reset clears the PIN and all PIN grants, withdraws trust in the external issuer and the stored owner tokens, turns off the outside face and voids its web sessions and one-time passcodes, revokes all outside grants, mutually recognised cards and paired devices, and records an audit entry; afterwards the PIN can only be set again on the local command line.
api.route.settings.pinReset.field.confir: Confirm the reset: it withdraws trust in the external issuer and the stored owner tokens, and revokes all outside grants, mutually recognised cards and paired devices
api.route.settings.pinReset.notLetIn: A reset only takes access back (revokes all outside grants, mutually recognised cards and paired devices) and lets nobody in; you reset only when you have forgotten the PIN, so it is done only on the local command line and needs no PIN
api.route.settings.pinReset.summary: Reset the PIN locally (clears the PIN and all PIN grants)
api.route.settings.pinSet.description: The first set needs no old PIN; after a local reset it can only be set again on this machine's command line. Once a PIN is set, changing it needs the old PIN, and a wrong old PIN counts toward consecutive wrong tries just like getting a grant. After a change, all previously issued PIN grants stop working. Daisy stores only a verifier of the PIN. Until the PIN is set, Daisy starts no AI turns.
api.route.settings.pinSet.notLetIn: Sets or changes the PIN itself (changing needs the old PIN; after a reset only the local command line can set it); lets nobody in
api.route.settings.pinStatus.description: Also gives the time and entry point of the most recent set and reset, which the web page and paired devices use to keep reminding the owner. While no PIN is set, Daisy starts no AI turns.
api.route.settings.pinStatus.summary: Show whether the PIN is set and whether it is locked
api.route.settings.relayOff.description: Connections going through the relay are cut immediately, and the card no longer carries the relay address. The key and certificate are kept (choosing the same relay again keeps the same address). It only narrows who can connect in, but still needs the PIN: a command-line credential may be the owner's AI using it through Bash, and it must not be able to quietly cut off the owner's reachability from other networks.
api.route.settings.relayOff.notLetIn: Stopping the relay only narrows who can connect in; still needs the PIN (the AI must not quietly disconnect the owner's relay)
api.route.settings.relayOff.summary: Stop using the relay: disconnect and remove the address from the card
api.route.settings.relaySet.description: Requests arriving through the relay only reach the outside face, so choosing a relay lets anyone who can reach the relay knock on the outside face's door: it needs the PIN. The outside face's listener does not need to be on first (relay-only works too); the outside face's passcode is turned on automatically. Certificate: by default one is requested from Let's Encrypt (TLS-ALPN-01, passed through the relay); before it arrives, or if it cannot be obtained, a self-signed certificate is used, and then only Daisy-to-Daisy traffic works through the relay (they check the TLS binding statement), while third-party clients and browsers report an untrusted certificate.
api.route.settings.relaySet.summary: Choose a relay (or switch): Daisy connects out and stays connected, getting a fixed outside address
api.route.settings.relayShow.summary: Show the relay: which one is chosen, whether it is connected, the outside address, the certificate
api.route.settings.show.description: When the outside face listens with a self-signed certificate, `external.fingerprint` is that certificate's SHA-256 fingerprint (DER, colon-separated hex, the same as openssl and browsers show): when the browser warns that the certificate is not trusted, continue only if it matches.
api.route.settings.show.summary: Show the two faces and the passcode: where they listen, where the port comes from, whether the passcode is on
api.route.settings.uiOriginsClear.descri: Narrows who can connect, no PIN needed (like turning off the outside face). Realtime channels already connected are disconnected at the next change.
api.route.settings.uiOriginsClear.notLet: Clears the external UI origins; only narrows who can connect
api.route.settings.uiOriginsClear.summar: Clear the allowed external UI origins
api.route.settings.uiOriginsSet.descript: A kind of "letting someone in": the listed web pages can carry a token the external issuer signed for the owner and, in the browser, call the local API and the realtime channel as the owner through the outside face (the local face does not accept them), so it needs the PIN and the AI cannot do it. Requests from these origins accept only tokens the external issuer gave the owner; web sessions and local credentials are always refused.
api.route.settings.uiOriginsSet.summary: Set the allowed external UI origins (replaces the whole list)
api.route.settings.uiOriginsShow.descrip: External UIs running in a browser (such as an organisation platform's web page) call the local API from these origins through the outside face (it applies only on the outside face; the local face accepts no other origin). A UI backend inside a server process sends no Origin and does not need this setting.
api.route.settings.uiOriginsShow.summary: Show the allowed external UI origins (external UIs in a browser, CORS)
api.route.settings.updateApply.descripti: Once fully idle: backs up the database first, keeps the current version's package as a fallback, runs `npm install -g` for the new version and checks that it loads, then restarts into the new version; if the new version is not running properly within 120 seconds, it rolls back automatically. Without `from`: the latest version in the source; `from`: a `.tgz` package on this machine. A version older than the one running needs `allowDowngrade`. Runs even when auto-update is off. Answers 409 `update_unavailable` when it cannot restart itself, is not a global npm install, or is already up to date.
api.route.settings.updateApply.field.all: Allow switching to a version older than the one running
api.route.settings.updateApply.field.fro: A .tgz package of @daisy-ai/daisy on this machine (absolute path)
api.route.settings.updateApply.notLetIn: Updates Daisy itself (no PIN, waits for idle, backs up first, can roll back, records an audit entry); lets nobody in
api.route.settings.updateApply.summary: Switch to a new version (waits for idle; Daisy installed via npm)
api.route.settings.updateCancel.notLetIn: Cancels an update restart; lets nobody in
api.route.settings.updateCancel.summary: Withdraw a restart request that has not run yet
api.route.settings.updateCheck.descripti: Checks once against the update source the owner set (`updateSource` in runner.json; there is no default source); if there is a newer version, fetches it into the data directory's `update/incoming/` and reads its version number, without installing. With no source set, or for a Daisy that is not a global npm install (such as a code checkout), answers 409 `update_unavailable`.
api.route.settings.updateCheck.notLetIn: Only checks whether there is a new version; lets nobody in
api.route.settings.updateCheck.summary: Check now for a new version (Daisy installed via npm)
api.route.settings.updateRestart.descrip: `idle` waits until no work is running, then restarts; `now` restarts immediately and interrupts turns in progress: it first answers 409, listing what would be interrupted and giving a `confirm` credential; it runs only when that credential is sent back (if new work starts in the meantime, it answers 409 again with a new list and a new credential). Interrupted work is not replayed.
api.route.settings.updateRestart.field.c: The confirm credential from the last 409: confirms interrupting the work on that list
api.route.settings.updateRestart.field.m: idle: wait for idle; now: immediately
api.route.settings.updateRestart.notLetI: Update and restart (no PIN, needs confirmation, records an audit entry); lets nobody in
api.route.settings.updateSourceSet.descr: There is no default source: unset, auto-update checks nothing. It can be a directory of `.tgz` files or one `.tgz` (absolute path), `npm:@daisy-ai/daisy[@tag]` (only for use once this scope is registered and the package published), or `off`; `null` removes it. The source decides what code this machine runs from then on, so it needs the PIN (any write does), and it is written to `updateSource` in runner.json.
api.route.settings.updateSourceSet.field: Directory, .tgz, npm:@daisy-ai/daisy@<tag>, off; null removes it
api.route.settings.updateSourceSet.notLe: Decides where Daisy's own new versions come from (it changes the code that runs later, so it needs the PIN); lets nobody in
api.route.settings.updateSourceSet.summa: Set the update source (needs the PIN)
api.route.settings.updateStatus.descript: Lists versions already installed or built that take effect once idle, the owner's restart request, and the sessions and commands running now that would be interrupted; a Daisy installed via npm also has `package`: the source, the new version found, the auto-update switch, and the result of the last update (switched / rolled back / failed, with the reason and the pre-update backup).
api.route.settings.updateStatus.summary: Show pending updates and restarts, and what they are waiting for
api.route.settings.webLogout.exempt: Logout for web sessions; the command line has no session to log out of
api.route.settings.webLogout.notLetIn: Voids your own web session credential; only narrows
api.route.settings.webLogout.summary: Web logout: void this session credential
api.route.settings.webSession.descriptio: Bring the one-time passcode from `daisy open`; on the local face, when the passcode is off, a same-origin web page can exchange without one. A one-time passcode can be used only once and is valid only on the face that issued it.
api.route.settings.webSession.exempt: Used by the web page to get its own session credential; the command line uses the local credential and does not need it
api.route.settings.webSession.notLetIn: The web page exchanges a one-time passcode for a session credential: the passcode itself is issued by an endpoint that needs the PIN (outside face) or by the local command line
api.route.settings.webSession.summary: Get a session credential for the web page
api.route.system.auditList.description: Paged from newest to oldest. Every local API action (except reads), every refusal, every tool the AI uses, and each handler's own domain records (such as pin.*, session.create) are here; records caused by the same action share a trace id. Only the owner can view it (web page, paired devices, command line); the AI's work credential cannot. Reading the audit is itself recorded too.
api.route.system.auditList.summary: View the audit: who, through which entry, did what to what, the result, the trace id
api.route.system.health.exempt: Read by the local commands daisy status and daisy doctor, not a subcommand of its own (local-api.md section 1: process-level commands)
api.route.system.health.summary: Health check: whether it is running, API version, release version
api.route.system.live.description: The first frame authenticates with a credential (the same checks as Bearer: command-line credential, web session; the AI's work credential cannot be used); after that, session events and changes are pushed per subscription; after a disconnect the client catches up by cursor. The upgrade request's Origin must be this face's own origin.
api.route.system.live.exempt: WebSocket push channel used inside the client package for live sync; the command line reads events by sequence number with daisy session events
api.route.system.locales.exempt: Used by the web page to fetch its own interface text (language pack); the command line reads the language pack directly
api.route.system.locales.field.areas: Only these areas (and their sub-areas; ui also fetches ui-chat etc.), comma-separated (e.g. ui,common); omitted = all
api.route.system.locales.summary: Get one language's interface text (its language pack)
api.route.system.logs.description: Log lines this process wrote recently (at most 1000 lines, cleared on restart; the full log is in the service manager, e.g. journalctl). Every line is already redacted; lines with a trace id can be matched against the audit. Only the owner can view them.
api.route.system.logs.summary: View recent logs (credentials, tokens and PIN redacted)
api.route.system.me.description: Single owner: the owner is the system account running Daisy. Answers which channel this request is recognised as (web page, paired device, command line) and which face it came in on (local face, outside face).
api.route.system.me.summary: Who am I: the owner, through which channel, on which face
api.route.system.tlsBinding.description: Public, no token needed (a2a-usage.md section 15.1). When another Daisy calls through a relay, it first fetches this, verifies the signature with the public key from its contacts, and compares it with the public key of the certificate on this connection; only if they match does it send its token: a relay can forge a trusted certificate for a subdomain, but it cannot sign this statement. Answers `application/jwt`: the header is exactly `{"alg":"EdDSA","typ":"daisy-tls-binding+jwt"}`, the payload `{ v: 1, id, spki: [...], iat, exp }`.
api.route.system.tlsBinding.exempt: Read by other Daisys' clients, not an owner command
api.route.system.tlsBinding.summary: TLS binding statement: "these TLS keys are mine", signed by this Daisy with its identity key
api.route.workspace.add.description: The path must be an absolute path on the runner, inside a root directory it allows.
api.route.workspace.add.field.label: Display name
api.route.workspace.browse.description: Asynchronous: answers with a request id; get the result with `workspace browse-result` (within 30 seconds). `ensure` creates the directory if it does not exist and registers it as a workspace.
api.route.workspace.browse.field.offset: Where to start listing the directory (paging)
api.route.workspace.browse.field.operati: browse: list a directory; ensure: make sure the directory exists and register it
api.route.workspace.browse.summary: Browse directories on a runner, or create and register a directory
api.route.workspace.browseResult.summary: Get the result of a directory request
api.route.workspace.catalog.summary: List the available runners, workspaces and your profiles
